content: Orf is an exanthematous disease caused by a parapoxvirus, primarily affecting sheep and goats. It is also referred to as contagious pustular dermatitis (CPD), sore mouth, contagious ecthyma, thistle disease, and scabby mouth. The orf virus is zoonotic, meaning it can infect humans as well. The term orf originates from Old English, where it means rough. Orf in Sheep and Goats Orf has been documented since the late 1800s and is prevalent in most regions where sheep and goats are raised, including Europe, the Middle East, the United States, Africa, Asia, Alaska, South America, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia. The disease spreads through direct contact or via fomites. In some cases, infection occurs through scratches caused by thistles, whether from growing or cut plants. Clinical signs in sheep and goats include papules and pustules on the lips and muzzle, and less commonly in the mouths of young lambs, as well as on the eyelids, feet, and teats of ewes. These lesions progress to thick crusts that may bleed. In lambs, oral lesions can interfere with suckling, leading to weight loss, and may also infect the ewe's udder, potentially causing mastitis. Sheep are susceptible to reinfection, and in some cases, the infection can become extensive and persistent if the animal fails to mount an adequate immune response. A live virus vaccine, derived from scab material, is available and is typically administered to ewes at two months of age. However, lambs are only vaccinated during outbreaks. The vaccine can cause disease in humans. In sheep and goats, lesions are most commonly found on or near the hairline, lips, and muzzle. In some cases, lesions may also appear in the nostrils, around the eyes, on the thighs, coronet, vulva, udder, and axilla. Rarely, lesions are observed in the tongue, gums, roof of the mouth, esophagus, or even the rumen. Severe cases have been reported, involving the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, heart, buccal cavity, cheeks, tongue, and lips. Another severe case involved pharyngitis, genital lesions, and hoof infections, leading to lameness and, in some instances, sloughing of the hoof. Typically, sheep recover from orf within a week or so as the disease resolves on its own. Caretakers can assist by applying antibiotic sprays to large scabs, ensuring infected lambs receive adequate milk, and isolating infected animals to reduce cross-transmission. It is recommended that individuals handling infected animals wear disposable gloves to prevent self-infection or cross-infection. Veterinarians should be consulted if there is a risk of misdiagnosis with other, more serious conditions. Orf in Humans Orf is a zoonotic disease, meaning humans can contract it through direct contact with infected sheep or goats or through fomites contaminated with the orf virus. In humans, the disease typically manifests as a purulent-appearing papule at the site of infection, without systemic symptoms. Commonly affected areas include the fingers, hands, arms, face, and, in rare cases, the penis (due to hand-to-genital transmission during urination). Good personal hygiene and the use of gloves when handling infected animals are essential to prevent infection. The papule may persist for 7 to 10 weeks and usually resolves spontaneously. Orf is an uncommon condition and is not easily recognized by most physicians. While it is generally a benign, self-limiting illness, it can become progressive and life-threatening in immunocompromised individuals. Topical 1% cidofovir has been successfully used in a few patients with progressive disease. If the eye becomes infected, even in healthy individuals, significant damage can occur. The virus can survive in soil for at least six months. Orf in Other Animals Although orf primarily affects sheep and goats, it has been reported as a natural disease in other species, including humans, steenbok, alpacas, chamois, thar, reindeer, musk ox, dogs, mountain goats, bighorn sheep, Dall sheep, and red squirrels.
